---
title: "Matrices — A Short Description of a Transformation"
description: "An original mathematical walkthrough with one running example, concrete numbers and a proof."
---

## Ask a simple question

Can we write the two-input machine T(x,y)=(2x+y,x−y) as a small table of numbers?

## Build the intuition

A matrix records the outputs of the basis directions as columns; multiplying by a vector combines those columns.

## Write the mathematical relationship

$$
\begin{bmatrix}2&1\\1&-1\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}3\\2\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}8\\1\end{bmatrix}
$$

**Every symbol explained:** The 2×2 table is matrix A; the column (3,2) is the input vector; the rightmost column is the output. Each output row is a dot product with the input column.

**Substitute real numbers:** First row: 2×3+1×2=8. Second row: 1×3+(−1)×2=1. This reproduces T(3,2)=(8,1).

## Why the relationship is true

The first column A(1,0)=(2,1), the second A(0,1)=(1,−1). Any (x,y)=x(1,0)+y(0,1), and linearity makes its output x times the first column plus y times the second.

## Where the shortcut stops working

A matrix represents a linear mapping relative to chosen bases. Simply adding 5 to every output is an affine transformation, not a linear one.

## Your turn

Predict the result for (1,2) using columns, then verify using row multiplication.

**Source structure:** Ivan Savov, *No Bullshit Guide to Linear Algebra*, second edition, Intro to linear algebra, §§2.3–2.5. This is an independently written explanation based on the uploaded **extended preview**, not a transcription of the commercial full book.
